The Program plays a key role as a neutral convener of organizations and individuals with disparate views about AI matters. The agency’s active participation in national and international discussions helps to shape the development of effective and reliable AI and ground AI governance in technical realities. The ITL AI Program has been engaged with U.S. and international AI governance efforts such as the OECD and the G7 Hiroshima Process, as well as a host of bilateral initiatives in places such as Asia, the Middle East, and North America. Using linked survey and administrative data, we produce tabulations of several intermediate imputation targets (e.g., filing rates, shares by filing status, numbers of dependents claimed, eligibility for key tax credits) for an array of tax unit types in the 2019 CPS ASEC. Data users can use these tables to improve imputations of tax variables in the public-use 2019 CPS ASEC. However, it is important to note that these intermediate values do not represent sample estimates of U.S. population characteristics. Technology Commercialization Fund The Technology Commercialization Fund (TCF) is a U.S. Department of Energy program that helps move innovations developed at DOE National Laboratories, plants, and sites into the marketplace. Established by Congress in the Energy Policy Act of 2005, TCF invests millions of dollars each year to bridge the gap between research and commercial application. The program supports partnerships between DOE facilities and industry, universities, and other organizations to advance technologies with strong market potential. By sharing costs with private and public partners, TCF strengthens the lab-to-market pipeline, fosters collaboration, and ensures that federally funded research delivers tangible benefits to the nation’s economy and energy security. pages.description: Nikkolas Smith, the bestselling illustrator, has a new children's book that takes a look at the innovative, creative dawn of our species.
pages.text: Telling the story of humanity’s origins in Africa—this time, for kids | National Geographic HISTORY & CULTURE Telling the story of humanity’s origins in Africa—this time, for kids Nikkolas Smith, the bestselling illustrator, has a new children's book that takes a look at the innovative, creative dawn of our species. The illustrator Nikkolas Smith, surrounded by his original canvas paintings for his new children's book, The History of We. Photograph By Vanessa Crocini By Kyndall Cunningham Published June 11, 2025 You’ve probably heard that we can all trace our roots back to Africa. It’s a fact that most people learn about briefly in a history class or find out through 23andMe. Still, this shared origin story often feels like a blip in our consciousness compared to other time periods. It’s a commonality we’re willing to acknowledge but not always explore. Picture-book author and film illustrator Nikkolas Smith fills in this curiosity gap with his latest book, The History of We , which he both wrote and illustrated. The self-described “artivist” has dedicated much of his career to rendering crucial moments and people in Black history through expressive paintings, from portraits of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor to a comic-book treatment of the Obamas. One of his most well-known projects is The 1619 Project: Born on the Water, the children’s adaptation of the New York Times venture led by Nikole-Hannah Jones, which he illustrated. With The History of We , Smith continues this tradition of documenting Black history in a way that’s accessible, honest, and completely mesmerizing.

Although indigenous peoples in North America have hunted wild turkeys since the end of the last Ice Age, the animals were first domesticated in Mexico around 2,000 years ago. Dinner wasn’t the original goal: archaeological evidence suggests turkeys were initially kept so their feathers could be used in clothing and ceremonial regalia. By A.D. 500, people were raising turkeys in what is now the United States too, judging by archaeological remains from caves in Arizona and New Mexico. Even so, those weren’t the birds that English settlers ate in the Thirteen Colonies. The domestic turkey descends from a southern Mexican bird that the Spanish took home in the 1500s. The birds then spread through Europe, and colonists brought them back across the Atlantic. The bird’s English name may reflect this long-distance trade: turkeys are thought to have reached England along winding trading routes that first passed through the country of Turkey. 2. Testing for Hepatitis B For Everyone Nov. 2, 2026 Key points Getting tested for hepatitis B is the only way to find out if you are infected. All adults and pregnant women should get tested for hepatitis B. People with ongoing risk need periodic testing. You can find out if you have hepatitis B through a blood test. Why get tested Many people with hepatitis B do not look or feel sick, so testing is the only way to know if you are infected. It's important to get tested for hepatitis B, so that if you are infected you can get medical care and avoid spreading the virus to others. Chronic, or long-term, hepatitis B can cause serious health problems, including liver damage, liver cancer, liver failure, and even death. pages.text: Tetanus is making a comeback. There’s an easy way to fight back. | National Geographic HEALTH Tetanus is making a comeback. There’s an easy way to fight back. It's easy to dismiss, but more Americans died from tetanus last year than any year in nearly two decades. The U.S. is seeing its highest tetanus case numbers in years. Experts blame falling vaccination rates. Mark Thiessen, National Geographic By Meryl Davids Landau Published June 4, 2026 In the classic tale of tetanus, a farmworker steps on an old barn nail and develops the bacterial disease. Most Americans don’t work on farms these days, so it’s easy for people to dismiss the illness as something they’re unlikely to encounter. In reality, this serious microbial infection can impact anyone anywhere, and more Americans are succumbing. Some 38 people came down with tetanus in 2025, the highest number in nearly 20 years. Experts blame declining vaccination rates and worry that case numbers will keep rising in the coming years if fewer people get the recommended shots. “These cases, while rare, are very troubling, because tetanus is totally preventable,” says Larry Madoff , an infectious disease physician at the Center on Emerging Infectious Diseases at Boston University. Madoff’s center first pointed to the concerning trend in a report published online late last year. For centuries, the permafrost protected the graves of men who hunted whales in the Arctic. But coastal erosion and melting ice now threaten to decay their remains. Under the unceasing light of polar summer, in a landscape of rock and ice, they hunted bowhead whales in the waters surrounding the Svalbard archipelago. The work was brutal; the wind unrelenting. Many never made it home. They were buried in whalers’ graveyards, fully dressed in their woolen jackets and knitted hats. Their shallow graves were marked with mounds of stones. pages.description: Scientists call the events permafrost detachment slides. Instead of thawing from the top down, these landslides seem to originate from a weakened base
pages.text: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a New Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms Skip to main content A scar left by the 2018 Redstone River permafrost landslide, one of the two events investigated in the new study. Adapted from J. M. Young et al., Geophysical Research Letters , 2026 In 2017 and 2018, a pair of strange landslides moved huge masses of rock and dirt in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The events occurred in the central Mackenzie Valley, and one of them even dammed a river and created a lake . The two natural disasters are part of a new class of landslides scientists are calling “permafrost detachment slides” in a study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters in September. They may have been partially triggered by severe wildfires that occurred in 1995, which destabilized the ground and allowed the base of the permafrost to thaw. What’s more, these events may become more common as the planet continues to warm. “It’s a very dramatic manifestation of the changing climate,” says study co-author Joseph Young , a geoscientist who conducted the work at the University of Alberta in Canada, to Matt Simon at Grist . “They’ve only started happening in the last 10, 15 years, and it’s a very drastic and abrupt change in the landscape.” Young and his colleagues began the study after seeing something strange in the Northwest Territories in 2019. While conducting field research, they spotted large landslide scars in valleys that they knew were stable permafrost , or permanently frozen earth, reports Stephanie Pappas for Live Science

pages.text: The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning - BBC Sport By Jessica Abrahams BBC World Service Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in. She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet. Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes. The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space. It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles. Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race. Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons. So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend? But many Premier League fans feel they are short-changed, locked out of many of their team's fixtures just because they live in this country. Learn about other national symbols. History of the American flag The flag of the United States is a symbol of freedom before which Americans recite the pledge of allegiance . The flag's 13 red and white stripes represent the 13 original colonies. Its 50 white stars on a blue background represent the 50 states. Each of the colors on the flag has a meaning: Red: valor and bravery White: purity and innocence Blue: vigilance, perseverance, and justice A star is added to the flag when a new state joins the United States. The flag was last modified on July 4, 1960, when Hawaii was incorporated as a state. Learn more about the evolution of the American flag and its earlier designs. How to raise the flag Follow these guidelines to properly display the American flag [PDF, 162KB]. When to fly the flag at half-staff The American flag flies at half-staff or at half-mast when the country or a state is in mourning. The president, a state governor, or the mayor of the District of Columbia can order flags to fly at half-staff. pages.text: The ancient Nigerian sculptures that rewrote African history | National Geographic HISTORY & CULTURE The ancient Nigerian sculptures that rewrote African history After a fragment was found in 1943 and dated to 500 B.C., the Nok terra-cotta sculptures shook up the Eurocentric academic consensus that no advanced cultures existed in sub-Saharan Africa that early. A life-size Nok terra-cotta discovered at the Ifana site in Nigeria. PETER BREUNIG By Carlos Micó Published July 27, 2026 In 1886, when Nigeria was a colony of the British Empire, the Royal Niger Company gained exclusive mineral rights over the Jos Plateau in central Nigeria, an area rich in tin ore and inhabited by the Berom people. In the foothills, access routes to the mines ran through an area called Nok. Over the years, with the exploitation of the mines and the local people who overwhelmingly provided the labor force, numerous fragments of ancient pottery came to light but were largely ignored. One piece, too striking to be disregarded, appeared in 1928: a small monkey head, sculpted in terra-cotta. The mine manager, Lt. Col. John Dent Young, had that piece and other fragments transferred to a museum in the city of Jos, the provincial capital. Fifteen years later, a miner found another terra-cotta head and took it home, where he used it as a scarecrow, apparently with some success. A British engineer noticed the piece about a year later, and brought it to Jos, where he showed it to Bernard Fagg, an archaeologist working in Nigeria as a civil administrator for the British Colonial Service. pages.description: Priestess of the moon god and daughter of Sargon the Great, Enheduanna amassed political power and waged war with her honeyed words.
pages.text: The Ancient Princess Who Crushed Enemies With Her Quick Tongue | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE The Ancient Princess Who Crushed Enemies With Her Quick Tongue Priestess of the moon god and daughter of Sargon the Great, Enheduanna amassed political power and waged war with her honeyed words. Enheduanna is often identified as the first author who appears independently in the historical record. Her hymns to the gods of Akkad and Sumer survived centuries after her death—and their translations are changing what modern scholars know about the role of women in the ancient Middle East. Photo Illustration, NGM Staff. Source Photo for Illustration: Yale Peabody Museum By Liddy Berman Published September 8, 2026 More than 4,000 years ago, Enheduanna, high priestess of the Sumerian moon god and daughter of a king, labored over a palm-size clay tablet. Reed stylus in her hand, she pressed its tiny wedge-shaped tip into the clay to build the small, spiky characters of cuneiform. She had been driven from her temple home by a rebel leader who opposed her family’s imperial rule over the kingdoms of Ur and Uruk. Though exiled and frightened, she was far from powerless—her words were believed to influence the gods. In her writings, Enheduanna petitioned her patron goddess— Inanna , the Mesopotamian deity of love, war and change—to rescue her from the dark fate awaiting political exiles and restore her to her rightful position as high priestess. pages.text: The ancient Romans' most expensive mistake in their hunt for silver | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE The most expensive mistake in ancient Roman history Two thousand years ago, the Roman Army embarked on a far-flung hunt for silver. A new discovery reveals how close they came to finding an empire-altering fortune. Roman money, like this coin bearing the profile of Emperor Claudius, often contained silver, one of several precious metals that fueled Rome. Photograph by Robert Kawka, Alamy Stock Photo By Julian Sancton Art by Aria Safarzadegan Published July 21, 2025 The passage is easy to miss. A paragraph-long anecdote in the Annals by the Roman historian Tacitus, it tells a story found nowhere else, about an unpopular legate forcing legionaries into a treacherous mine at the frontier of the empire. It takes place during the reign of Claudius (A.D. 41–54), a time of furious expansion when Rome sought to swallow up the borderlands and their resources. The location mentioned in the Tacitus passage is vague, described as “in the district of Mattium,” just outside of Roman-occupied Germania Superior . But the goal is clear: to find more of a metal that powered the realm. ( Female Gladiators? Tantalizing New Evidence From Ancient Rome) Silver trickled down from patricians, officers, and soldiers to the rest of the economy, in the form of coins and ingots and jewelry. pages.text: The Artisans Trying to Bring Back Neolithic Fashion | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE The Artisans Trying to Bring Back Neolithic Fashion A growing community of craftspeople are trying to build knowledge of ancient clothing—by making it themselves. Historical craft specialist Vasi Birchwood recreates fashion from the Neolithic period on her Youtube channel. This outfit is one of her creations. The jacket is made of deer skin, stitched with deer skin cord and a bone awl, and adorned with moose teeth. The shirt underneath the jacket is made of undyed linen, hand stitched with linen thread. The skirt is made of deer skin and decorated with braided hemp strings. Photo Illustration: NGM Staff; Source Photos for Illustration: Vasi Birchwood By Starre Vartan Published November 2, 2026 Around the fire, no one seems especially bothered by the rain. Some people duck beneath bark shelters to continue twisting cordage from plant fibers. Others cook foraged plants or work leather while steam rises from damp clothing. A few wander into the drizzle to gather more wood before returning to the warmth of the flames. Among them is historical craft specialist and YouTube educator Vasi Birchwood . For Birchwood, weather isn't an inconvenience so much as another participant in this meeting of experiential archeologists and craft experts in Northern Germany. That shift in perspective is just one of the many ways she does more than dress like a Neolithic person at these gatherings. pages.text: The Astronomical Problem of Space Junk Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Images by Samantha Lawler / NASA / smspsy via Adobe Stock and public domain We have launched all manner of satellite and machinery into low-Earth orbit. But what goes up must come down. Most often, these items burn up in the atmosphere upon re-entry, which isn’t good for air quality or the ozone layer. But not everything incinerates — and increasing amounts of debris are hurtling back toward Earth and landing in backyards and farm fields. Falling detritus disrupts air travel and risks collision with infrastructure and people on the ground. There are those who argue that additional regulation is required around the launching and de-orbiting of these materials. In this episode, host Ari Daniel speaks with astronomer Samantha Lawler and Smithsonian contributing writer Dan Falk about space junk and the concern among researchers that it is becoming a growing threat to public safety. The continent of North America has been inhabited by humans for at least 16,500 years. As early as the 1500s, early settlers and European thinkers were interested in discovering how humans had come to populate North and South America. One theory suggested the migration of Norsemen across Greenland into North America. Another theory proposed the island of Atlantis as the origins of human life in the New World. Yet another idea proposed that the inhabitants had generated out of mud. However, by the early 1800s, scientists and theorists began discussing the possibility of a land bridge that had spanned between Asia and North America thousands of years ago. Anthony Brown, Alamy By Tristan Kennedy Published November 8, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Renowned for its distinctive skiing culture, Japan is the ultimate wish list destination for serious skiers and snowboarders. If you’re used to the slopes of Europe or North America, you’ll appreciate the small differences: in the menu at a mountain cafe, the particular etiquette of the onsen, or even the heated toilet seats; everything feels different in Japan. But the main claim to fame is its soft, lightweight and very consistent powder snow. Westerly winds whip off the Siberian tundra and scoop up moisture over the Sea of Japan, before dumping it as snow over the archipelago. This quirk of geography means that parts of the northern island of Hokkaido are blessed with up to 15 metres of snowfall every winter compared to, say, seven metres in European resorts such as Tignes, France. Replenished near-daily, fluffy Japanese snow is incredibly forgiving for skiers and boarders, earning it a special nickname among aficionados: ‘Ja-pow’. But it’s not always easy to get enough, especially if you follow a plant-based diet. Protein is an essential building block for life and a staple of our diet. However, not all sources of protein are equally beneficial to our health. Photograph by fcafotodigital, Getty Images By Joel Mathis Published September 13, 2024 Protein is a really important component of a proper diet. You might be familiar with the role it plays in helping you build muscle and feeling full after a meal—but that’s not all it can do. “Protein plays a crucial role to our physiology,” says Jessica Corwin, lead registered dietician at Corewell Health, a hospital group in Michigan. Protein-rich foods provide amino acids that the body uses to build and repair tissues, power the immune system, and even help regulate hormones. The recommended daily allowance is based on your body weight: About 0.36 grams for every pound that you weigh. That’s about 54 grams of protein a day for a 150-pound person. ( How much protein do you really need ?) But it’s not always easy to get enough protein—especially if you’re trying to follow a plant-based diet. Different people also need different amounts of protein depending on their gender, health status, activity level, and age. So what are the best sources of protein? Here’s what the experts say. pages.title: The best summers of my life were spent at the Grand Canyon Lodge. Now it’s gone. | National Geographic
pages.description: Built nearly 100 years ago, the remote lodge offered majestic views of one of our finest national parks before it burned in the Dragon Bravo Fire.
pages.text: The best summers of my life were spent at the Grand Canyon Lodge. Now it’s gone. | National Geographic By Leath Tonino Published July 18, 2025 I’m not usually one to get weepy over a hotel, let alone a patio and some rough-hewn wooden furniture. But when Arizona’s famous Grand Canyon Lodge and a number of smaller adjacent structures burned down on the night of July 12 in the Dragon Bravo Fire, a blaze that to date has consumed 11,344 acres and remains entirely uncontained, it left a hole in more than just the conifer forest of the North Rim . My heart, my friends’ hearts—there’s a hole in each of these now. And there are similar holes in the hearts of thousands of folks across the globe who also loved, and still love, and will forever love, that rustic palace, that gobsmacking view, that superlative place. ( Grand Canyon National Park Photos) In 2024, close to five million visitors experienced the beauty and wonder of Grand Canyon National Park , but only ten percent of them ventured to the high, green, thrillingly remote North Rim. For those that did make the five-hour drive from Las Vegas, or the six-hour drive from Flagstaff, or the seven-hour drive from Salt Lake City, the Grand Canyon Lodge, which until this past weekend perched at an elevation of 8,000 feet near the tip of Bright Angel Point, was invariably the destination. Designed by architect Gilbert Stanley Underwood and built in 1928 with local ponderosa pine and Kaibab Limestone, it was destroyed in 1932 thanks to a runaway kitchen fire.
